text: If Earth's magnetic field switched off right now, your compass would stop pointing north.
That field comes from liquid iron swirling in Earth's core, about three thousand kilometres down.
It's a shield. The Sun blows a wind of charged particles at us, about four hundred kilometres a second.
The field bends that wind around us. Without it, the wind hits our air directly.
Satellites and astronauts take the first hit, from a lot more radiation.
Sea turtles, salmon and some birds use the field to navigate. They'd get lost.
But on the ground, you'd be mostly fine. The thick air above you is a second shield.
The real danger is slow. The solar wind would strip away our upper atmosphere, bit by bit.
That's what happened to Mars. Its field died billions of years ago, and it lost most of its air.
But that took hundreds of millions of years. And Earth's stronger gravity holds on tighter.
And forty-one thousand years ago, the field really did drop below a tenth of today's strength.
Life carried on. The magnetic poles have even swapped places hundreds of times.
So thank the hot iron under your feet. It keeps the lazy Sun's wind out of your hair.
